https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c54g.text: Image source, Reuters By Jessica Rawnsley Published 8 hours ago The lone holdout juror in the trial of Lindsay Clancy has said he "didn't have any doubts" that she was criminally responsible for killing her three children. "Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned it," Michael Desronvil said in a statement to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. The judge declared a mistrial on 4 September after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict following nearly 40 hours of deliberating. Clancy admitted to the killings but her lawyers argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. Prosecutors said the killings were calculated. Warning: This article contains distressing details The 36-year-old was charged with three counts of first-degree murder after strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home before jumping out of the second-floor window. To find Clancy guilty, jurors had to be unanimously convinced beyond reasonable doubt that she intentionally killed her children and that she did not do so as a result of postpartum psychosis, a rare and serious condition. The jury - nine women and three men - considered a range of options including not guilty by reason of insanity, manslaughter and first-degree murder. Several jurors have said following the mistrial being declared that the panel was ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible. Desronvil said he believed the evidence presented in court showed she had planned the killings. "I didn't have any doubts," he said in a statement to CBS on Thursday. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented." 'Emotional rollercoaster' - Lindsay Clancy jurors speak out on what led to mistrial Published 9 September What happens next after Lindsay Clancy's murder case ends in a mistrial? Published 5 September Paula Devlin, one of the other jurors, told CBS Mornings that the panel had spent several days trying to convince Desronvil to change his mind. "We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2," she said. The jury foreperson, a retired fifth-grade teacher, described not being able to reach a verdict as "awful" and an "emotional rollercoaster". She told NBC that Desronvil had "admitted he had reasonable doubt", but as she started filling out the verdict sheets, he apparently said: "But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity." Another juror told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors had been "very firm in their stance" from the start and "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side". But they added that because Desronvil would not "follow" his reasonable doubt nor offer logical reasoning for his position, they felt Clancy had not received a fair trial. The identities of all 11 jurors have not been officially disclosed but in the US, once a case is over, any juror can choose to speak publicly about a case and their deliberations. Figure caption, Watch: Patrick Clancy's current wife describes him as 'selfless father' Patrick Clancy, the children's father and Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband, is due to speak publicly about the case in an interview with the CBS programme 60 Minutes on Sunday. In it, he is expected to discuss his grief, his memories of his children and the conspiracy theories that have flooded social media since the trial began. He said he still speaks to his children "all the time", describing it as "a way I stay connected to them". During the trial, Clancy's defence team had attempted to use her being put on more than a dozen medications in the lead-up to the killings, as well as seeking help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room, as evidence of her psychosis. Postpartum psychosis can involve hallucinations and delusions, and her lawyers argued that she was unable to understand the nature of her actions or distinguish right from wrong. A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence said Clancy experienced a "command hallucination" and a "delusion of influence" when she killed her children. However, her psychiatrist testified for the prosecution that Clancy did not show signs of psychosis during their sessions , while another psychiatrist noted that the condition was not currently recognised by the American Psychiatric Association. Under Massachusetts law, prosecutors had to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible for the jury to find her guilty. The defence did not have to prove her mental illness or lack of criminal responsibility. The mistrial leaves the case unresolved. Prosecutors have not said whether they will seek a retrial. Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, has said he hopes to reach an agreement with prosecutors to avoid a second trial. He told ABC's Good Morning America that he was upset that the lone juror would not acquit Clancy. He said the holdout "would not apply the law of reasonable doubt" as instructed by the judge, adding: "That's not right. And that's why I was upset." The next court hearing is scheduled for 29 September at Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts. https://www.politico.eu/article/leader-f.text: Finland’s President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a joint call with Russian leader Vladimir Putin on Tuesday as part of international efforts to secure an end to the war in Ukraine. “The discussion was frank and substantive,” said Stubb said in a statement after the call. “We are neighboring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions.” The two leaders — who are firm allies of Ukraine — were not speaking as official representatives of Europe as a whole, and the conversation was held in consultation with Kyiv. Advertisement Advertisement Støre said the European leaders stressed the importance of de-escalation in the call with Putin. “The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations,” he added. Their conversation comes at a highly sensitive moment as U.S. President Donald Trump pushes for a peace deal. Talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine are planned to take place in Abu Dhabi next month. Stubb’s office described the call as a follow-up to talks in Oslo on Oct. 20 , in which the two European leaders were joined by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, who then traveled to meet Putin in Russia the following day. Stubb and Støre are close friends and speak frequently, and they were together in Helsinki for the conversation with Putin. According to a statement from the Finnish president’s office, the two leaders wanted to tell the Russian leader directly that they would continue supporting Ukraine and that peace negotiations must resume, looking ahead to the planned meetings in Abu Dhabi. They also told the Russian leader that they had a shared interest in the stability of the Baltic Sea region and the High North. The last staunch European supporter of Ukraine to speak to Putin at leader level is believed to have been French President Emmanuel Macron in 2025. Some EU leaders like Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico and former Hungarian premier Viktor Orban have maintained semi-regular contact with the Russian president in recent years, despite the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Advertisement Advertisement EU diplomats and officials have been considering how to ensure Ukraine’s allies in Europe can play a meaningful part in negotiations on a ceasefire and longer term peace agreement. Stubb’s name emerged as one of the potential leaders who could take on the job of representing Europe and bolstering Ukraine in face-to-face talks with Trump and Putin. He is one of the few EU leaders and Ukraine backers who has maintained a healthy relationship with Trump at a time of strained relations across the Atlantic. Finland also shares a 1,300 kilometer border with Russia, meaning Stubb and his officials already have valuable experience of dealing with a threatening and unpredictable neighbor. https://hvg.hu/vilag/20261116_orizetbe-v.text: Az FSZB szerint az orosz állampolgárságú gyanúsított „az ukrán titkosszolgálatok megbízásából részt vett egy közéleti személyiség és független újságíró (...) autójának felrobbantásában”. Az orosz Szövetségi Biztonsági Szolgálat (FSZB) őrizetbe vett hétfőn egy 21 éves nőt, aki részese volt egy gépkocsi felrobbantásával elkövetett merényletnek. A támadás célpontja Mikola Azarov ukrán exminiszterelnök egykori tanácsadója, Szergej Zavorotnij volt, aki súlyosan megsebesült. Az FSZB szerint az orosz állampolgárságú gyanúsított „az ukrán titkosszolgálatok megbízásából részt vett egy közéleti személyiség és független újságíró (...) autójának felrobbantásában”. A közlemény szerint a nőt csalók rávették egy nagyobb összeg átutalására egy általa biztonságosnak gondolt számlára, amit a bűnözők eszközként használtak fel arra, hogy további nyomást gyakoroljanak rá. A robbantás pénteken történt az orosz fővárosban, a sebesült Zavorotnijt pedig a városi kórházba szállították. Az ügyben emberölési kísérlet címén indítottak büntetőeljárást. Azarov később közölte, hogy volt tanácsadójának állapota válságos, és azzal vádolta meg Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnököt, hogy személyesen hagyja jóvá azoknak a személyeknek a listáját, akik ellen a közvetlenül őalá rendelt ukrán szolgálatok merényleteket készítenek elő. Szergej Zavorotnij a Komszomolszkaja Pravda című orosz lapnál dolgozott, 2003-2004-ben a Rogyina párt frakciójának sajtószolgálatát vezette az orosz parlamentben, majd az ukrán miniszterelnöki posztot 2010-től 2014-ig betöltő Azarov sajtótitkára lett, a később megdöntött Viktor Janukovics elnöksége alatt. 2014 februárjában Azarov elhagyta Ukrajnát, és Oroszországba távozott, ahová Zavorotnij követte őt, és a volt kormányfő által alapított Ukrajna Megmentésének Bizottsága nevű mozgalom sajtótitkára lett. Társszerzője volt egy Oroszországban kiadott könyvnek, amely az ukrajnai erőszakos hatalomátvételről szól. Zavorotnijt az amerikai hírszerzés az FSZB tisztjeként azonosította, aki részt vett az orosz szolgálatok műveletében, amelynek célja a 2016-os amerikai választások befolyásolása volt. 2019-ben egy ukrán bíróság Zavorotnijt távollétében 13 év börtönre ítélte hazaárulásért, később pedig felkerült Kijev szankciós listájára is, egykori főnökével, Azarovval együtt. Akár 15 év börtönt is kaphat a korrupciós pénzt több ügyféltől is a gyanú szerint elfogadó hivatali dolgozó.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: A satellite image of the Kerch bridge, which appears to have sustained a level of damage that ‘cannot be repaired any time soon’, according to a former commanding general of the US army in Europe. Photograph: VANTOR/Reuters View image in fullscreen A satellite image of the Kerch bridge, which appears to have sustained a level of damage that ‘cannot be repaired any time soon’, according to a former commanding general of the US army in Europe. Photograph: VANTOR/Reuters Ukraine Analysis ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play Dan Sabbagh Kyiv Partial demolition of bridge linking Russia and occupied Crimea is obvious embarrassment to Putin days before meeting with Xi and Trump Europe live – latest updates Tue 17 Nov 2026 11.40 EST Last modified on Tue 17 Nov 2026 15.37 EST Share Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long-range drones. The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing , one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. Such is the collapse of a span of the roadway, and the loss of its supporting arch above, it appears to be a level of damage that “cannot be repaired any time soon”, says Ben Hodges, a former commanding general of the US army in Europe . The 19km (12-mile), $3.6bn (£2.7bn) road bridge connecting Russia to the east of Crimea was completed in 2018, a project closely associated with Putin and his efforts to secure the 2014 annexation of Crimea by opening up a supply route to the peninsula. Russia’s leader was filmed driving an orange truck into Crimea, greeted by cheering workers once the construction was complete. “Putin initiated this project himself,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said at the time. That was four years before Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which has, if anything, made Russia’s position in Crimea more precarious, though the change in the balance of power is a while coming. 0:34 Ukraine releases footage of strike on Crimean Bridge – video Russia was able to bomb anywhere in Ukraine in 2022, while Kyiv was denied long-range western missiles, particularly those powerful enough to strike such a politically sensitive and strategic target. Instead, Ukraine tried to blow the bridge up with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone attack a year later. Neither did much long-term damage. It was only as Ukraine’s own long-range drones and cruise missiles came to fruition near the beginning of 2026 that a knockout strike became possible. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that the culminating attacks on the bridge, the end of two days of strikes, involved Ukrainian-made Neptune and Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles, Palianytsia rocket drones plus Ruta cruise missiles from the Dutch manufacturer Destinus, the only foreign arms company confirmed as involved. It was, the Ukrainian president said, the “seventh stage” in an operation “carried out over several weeks”. Radars, jamming equipment and air defence systems were progressively neutralised, opening up corridors of attack. Meanwhile, Russia had already started what is becoming a battle of the bridges. Moscow attacked Kyiv’s busy Northern and Southern bridges in early October, part of its scaled-up campaign against the capital and the country’s other large cities. Russia is struggling to make progress on the frontline, and a record 50,000 troops were killed or seriously wounded in October, according to the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte. Its efforts are focused on knocking out Ukraine’s electricity, heating and water supplies, though attacking bridges show its target list is expanding in grim desperation. Yet the Kremlin has chosen this expansion at a time when Ukraine can strike back. The pro-war Russian military blogger Military Informant notes that Ukraine has a “parity in firepower”, having downed the Kerch road bridge in two days of air raids. “It cannot be ruled out that the railway section will be destroyed next,” the blogger adds. If anything, further attacks on the bridge are almost certain both to prevent its repair and to make resupplying Crimea more difficult. Cutting the bridge entirely, rail and road, would leave Moscow with only the R-280 land highway from Rostov to Crimea, already the subject of months of Ukrainian drone attacks. Map Hodges has long argued that Crimea could be a defining theatre of the war, because “of what Crimea represents to Putin”. Ukraine should try to make “Russian occupation untenable” by destroying the bridge and asserting fire control over the R-280, he adds. A supply squeeze, however, is a slow process, though its political benefits may be felt more quickly. Bringing down the road bridge “further kills the narrative that Russian victory is inevitable or that Crimea is theirs”, Hodges says, although Trump may not bring up the episode in his meeting with Putin and Xi on Thursday. The danger is that both sides, in their desperation to end a deadlocked war, will escalate further. However, cut out of the talks in Shenzen, Zelenskyy had little choice but to remind Trump as well as Putin that Ukraine still has cards to play. Emily Ferris, a Russia expert with the Rusi thinktank, says Ukraine’s military-industrial complex was ready for some months, meaning the timing of the attack on the Kerch bridge can be interpreted only as political. “They were keeping it for a rainy day, and that day has come,” she said.
